patient.chief_complaint: DWI restriction on MRI after headache episode — 'confirmed migrainous infarction' — seeking second opinion
patient.hpi:
A 38-year-old Indian-British woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic for a second opinion following an MRI scan 3 weeks ago. She had an episode 4 weeks ago of visual disturbance in her left peripheral field (shimmering zigzag arc expanding over 20 minutes) followed by a severe right-sided headache lasting 12 hours. When the headache had not fully resolved by day 3, she attended a walk-in clinic, where MRI was arranged. The radiologist reported 'a 4mm area of DWI restriction in the right posterior watershed territory — acute infarction — possible migrainous infarction.' She was started on clopidogrel 75 mg daily and aspirin 75 mg (dual antiplatelet) by the local neurology team who were concerned about migrainous infarction.

She has a 10-year history of migraine with visual aura. She has 2-4 episodes per month, all with typical expanding visual aura over 15-25 minutes followed by right-sided headache. Her neurological symptoms have always been fully reversible after each episode. She had a combined OCP stopped 10 years ago when her migraines were first diagnosed and is now on a progestin-only pill (Cerazette). She is very concerned about the MRI finding and is currently not driving (advised by the previous team).

On review of the MRI images at this clinic: the 4mm DWI lesion is located in the right occipital cortex, and the ADC map shows corresponding low signal (genuine restricted diffusion) — this is a real acute infarction. However, the timing (day 3 post-episode), size, and location require careful interpretation.

Dual antiplatelet with clopidogrel — requires review

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Migrainous infarction (ICHD-3 1.4.1) — small right occipital cortical infarct during established visual aura; all secondary causes excluded; DAPT not indicated long-term

differential.diagnosis: Cardioembolic stroke during a coincidental migraine episode
differential.key_features: Critical alternative — must be excluded with prolonged cardiac monitoring, echo, and bubble study; ILR/Holter normal, echo normal
Bubble echo to evaluate — if PFO and cryptogenic stroke, closure may be considered
No neck pain or trauma; MRA shows no dissection
ESR/CRP normal; antiphospholipid panel pending; repeat at 12 weeks if borderline

useless_tools.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
EEG is not indicated for migraine with aura; reserve for cases where focal seizure is genuinely on the differential

critical_actions: Confirm migrainous infarction by ICHD-3 1.4.1 criteria (aura >60 min + infarct on imaging in the relevant territory)
Complete stroke-aetiology workup (MRA, prolonged cardiac monitoring, echo with bubble study, antiphospholipid antibodies)
Stop triptans permanently after migrainous infarction
Step down DAPT to single antiplatelet per stroke secondary-prevention guidance
Counsel that combined OCP must remain stopped
contraindicated_actions: Do not continue triptans after migrainous infarction
Do not continue dual antiplatelet therapy long-term in the absence of an ongoing indication
Do not restart combined oestrogen-progestogen contraception
key_reasoning_points: Migrainous infarction is a diagnosis of exclusion — competing aetiologies (cardioembolic, dissection, vasculitis, paradoxical embolism) must be ruled out first
Long-term DAPT is not standard after small cortical infarct — step down to single antiplatelet per current stroke guidance
Triptans are contraindicated permanently after migrainous infarction

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: DAPT is appropriate short-term post-stroke but should be stepped down to single antiplatelet long-term in this case

mri.impression: 4 mm area of restricted diffusion in the right occipital cortex — confirmed acute cortical infarction. Corresponding ADC low signal confirms true restriction. No other DWI lesions. Normal posterior circulation MRA — no PCA stenosis or vertebral dissection. Appearances consistent with a small cortical infarction in the right occipital territory

ELECTROCARDIOGRAM
RHYTHM: Sinus rhythm 68 bpm. QTc: 402 ms. No AF. Normal ECG.

sumatriptan.proposed: Continuation of sumatriptan 100 mg PRN for acute migraine after confirmed migrainous infarction
interactions: Sumatriptan + clopidogrel/aspirin: no pharmacokinetic interaction, but the vasoconstrictor mechanism of triptans is the concern, not an antiplatelet interaction
Sumatriptan + desogestrel (progestin-only): no clinically significant interaction
contraindications: Triptans (sumatriptan and all 5-HT1B/1D agonists) are CONTRAINDICATED after migrainous infarction and in patients with established cerebrovascular disease — they cause cranial vasoconstriction and may extend or precipitate ischaemia
Ergotamine and other ergot derivatives are likewise contraindicated for the same vasoconstrictive reason
warnings: Sumatriptan must be stopped PERMANENTLY following migrainous infarction; document the contraindication prominently in the record
Combined oestrogen-containing contraception must remain stopped (additional ischaemic risk in migraine with aura); the current progestin-only pill is acceptable
Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) should be stepped down to a single agent at 21-90 days per stroke secondary-prevention guidance — long-term DAPT is not indicated
alternatives: Acute migraine: NSAIDs (e.g. naproxen) or a CGRP-receptor antagonist (gepant, e.g. rimegepant) which lack vasoconstrictor activity and are not contraindicated post-infarction
Antiemetic adjunct (metoclopramide or prochlorperazine) for associated nausea
Initiate migraine preventive therapy (e.g. candesartan, amitriptyline, or topiramate) rather than relying on acute treatment

output.query: migrainous infarction ICHD-3 management antiplatelet DAPT clopidogrel prevention

results.source: ICHD-3; ESO stroke guidelines; Cephalalgia review
results.finding: ICHD-3 1.4.1 migrainous infarction: stroke during migraine aura; infarction in area corresponding to aura; no other stroke cause. Aspirin 75-150 mg daily for secondary prevention (weak evidence; extrapolated from ischaemic stroke). DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel): POINT/CHANCE trials support short-term DAPT for high-risk TIA; for migrainous infarction DAPT benefit unproven — current guidelines do not support long-term DAPT. Combined OCP absolutely contraindicated. Migraine prevention CRITICAL — preventing migraine prevents infarction; topiramate (Level A), propranolol (Level A), anti-CGRP antibodies. Triptans cautioned — weak evidence, individualised decision.
results.evidence_level: ICHD-3 consensus; ESO guidelines; Level A (preventives)

output.query: triptans migrainous infarction safety contraindication EHF guidelines

results.finding: Triptans are vasoconstrictors; after migrainous infarction, theoretical concern about vasoconstriction in a susceptible territory. No randomised trials specifically address triptan use after migrainous infarction; case reports rare and contradictory. EHF and EFNS caution against triptans but evidence base is weak. Untreated severe migraine attacks cause significant suffering and may trigger further CSD. 2022 EHF guidelines suggest weighing individual risk vs benefit — if infarction was small and well-characterised, cautious triptan use may be acceptable with monitoring. Prioritise strong preventive therapy to reduce acute treatment need.

output.summary: Triptans cautioned (not absolutely contraindicated) after migrainous infarction; prioritise preventive therapy to reduce acute treatment need; shared decision-making

output.query: driving DVLA restrictions migrainous infarction stroke 1 month visual field

results.source: DVLA At a Glance Guide (UK); DVLA medical standards
results.finding: After TIA or stroke with full recovery, DVLA regulations require a 1-month driving cessation period; resumption is permitted when there is no visual field defect on perimetry, no persisting neurological deficit, and no uncontrolled AF. Migrainous infarction is treated as a stroke for DVLA licensing purposes — the 1-month restriction applies. Formal visual field assessment is required before driving resumption is documented.

output.summary: UK DVLA regulations require a 1-month driving cessation after TIA/stroke; resumption requires documented full neurological recovery, no visual field defect on formal perimetry, and no uncontrolled AF; migrainous infarction is classified as a stroke for DVLA purposes
